quotes.text: That's why the industry calls the term a misnomer, because serverless was never about deleting servers. It was about deleting your responsibility for them.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Corrects the misleading name in one memorable line.

quotes.text: Serverless doesn't delete complexity. It moves it. Your team still deals with identity, networking, security, and the bill at the end of the month.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: An honest reminder of what stays the customer's responsibility.

quotes.text: You're not renting capacity, you're buying completed work. And that's a very different relationship with the bill.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Captures the shift in the cost model in one sentence.

quotes.text: Ask whether the job can finish quickly and ask whether it only needs to run when something happens. Two yes answers point you towards serverless.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: A simple two-question fit test listeners can apply right away.

quotes.text: Serverless means renting moments of work instead of machines, so the bill follows the work rather than the clock.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: A concise summary of the whole idea.

takeaways: Serverless does not remove servers; it removes your responsibility for running, patching and scaling them, and you pay for executions instead of idle machines.
Power Automate, Logic Apps and Azure Functions are serverless building blocks that can call each other, so you can start low code and add code only where needed.
Serverless fits short, event-triggered jobs, while cold starts, statelessness, lock-in, time limits and runaway costs make steady long-running work a poor fit.
hook: Many teams pay for virtual machines that sit idle most of the day, and the word serverless makes the alternative sound more mysterious than it is. This episode explains serverless computing in plain language, shows where it already runs in Power Automate, Logic Apps and Azure Functions, and names its limits and typical mistakes. Business users and beginners get a simple test for when serverless fits and a low-risk first step.
